findings.claim: For AQA Paper 2, you will have a printed extract from Leave Taking. You may be asked to write about a theme, a character, or a dramatic method, drawing on both the extract and the whole play. Both tasks reward AO1 (personal response), AO2 (methods) and AO3 (context). ... Extract analysis strategy: Work through the extract methodically ... Quote precisely from the printed passage.
findings.truth: The modern-text question is closed book with NO printed extract. Students answer one essay question from a choice of two on their studied modern prose or drama text. It is worth 30 marks plus 4 marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar (AO4). This is the single most damaging error in the unit: it tells students to revise for a task that does not exist and not to memorise quotations.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md - 'Section A Modern texts: students will answer one essay question from a choice of two on their studied modern prose or drama text'; and 'All assessments are closed book: any stimulus materials required will be provided as part of the assessment'. The spec's extract-based provision is described only for the 19th-century novel question. Paper 2 total 96 marks = 30+4 (modern text) + 30 (poetry) + 24+8 (unseen).

findings.claim: Enid speaks predominantly in standard English - the language of assimilation ... But when she is emotional, stressed or speaking about Jamaica, her language shifts: Jamaican patois breaks through the English surface. (Repeated across the lesson, its knowledge checks and five flashcards.)
findings.truth: Enid speaks Jamaican patois throughout the play. Every line of hers quoted in the published study material is in patois: 'I proud a my girls', 'England been good to me', 'I work jobs seven days a week' (Scene 2), 'the poorest family in the whole a Jamaica' (Scene 4), 'In a way, we poorer than them' (Scene 8), 'He's a high man. It look bad that Viv and Del wasn't here?' (Scene 3). The irony Pinnock builds is that Enid demands English respectability from her daughters in a voice that will never sound English; it is her London-born daughters who speak English. A student writing the lesson's version would misread every Enid speech.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy (AQA programme), 'Enid: England been good to me' lesson - emphasises Enid's use of Jamaican Patois, with the quoted lines above; Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract for Leave Taking (2024), quoted ENID lines from Scenes 2 and 3.

findings.claim: The play has two physical settings: Enid's North London living room (Scenes 2-5) and Mai's Deptford bedsit (Scenes 1, 6, 7, 8). (Same claim in lesson 6 content, its knowledge check options and two flashcards, and in lesson 1's matching knowledge check.)
findings.truth: Scene 5 is set at Mai's bedsit, not at Enid's. By Scene 5 the action has skipped forward a few weeks, Del is living with Mai, Mai reads Del's palm and identifies her dyslexia, and Viv comes to Mai's to tell Del she has walked out of her English Literature A-level. The correct split is Enid's home = Scenes 2-4, Mai's bedsit = Scenes 1 and 5-8.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas board knowledge-organiser for Leave Taking (resource.download.wjec.co.uk .../eduqas/leave-taking.pdf): 'Scene 5 - This scene skips forward a few weeks with Del living with Mai ... Viv comes to visit'; Oak National Academy 'An exploration of Scene Five': 'Scene Five takes place at Mai's home, with Del and Mai present'.

findings.claim: The news arrives via another letter - confirming what Enid had feared and half-denied since Scene 1. (Flashcard: 'Enid learns by letter that her mother has died in Jamaica.')
findings.truth: The news of Mooma's death comes by telephone in Scene 3. Viv answers a call from Enid's sister in Jamaica; the stage direction reads 'As ENID listens something drains out of her. She drops the phone'. The dropped phone is one of the play's best-known stage images, so the lesson removes the very moment a student would quote.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract, Scene Three: 'Enid receives a phone call from Cynthia informing her that Mooma has died', with the quoted stage direction (page 40); WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 3: 'Viv answers a phone call from her aunt who rings to tell the family that Enid's mother has died'.

findings.claim: set in 1984 London (three times in lesson 1, once in lesson 8); 'Scene 1 takes place on Easter Monday, 1984' (lesson 1) and 'on Easter Monday' (lesson 2); knowledge check 'In what year is Leave Taking set?' keyed to 1984 with 1987 offered as a wrong answer; flashcard 'London in 1984.'
findings.truth: The play is set in 1980s London. No board or publisher source gives a year, and none mentions Easter. Nick Hern's own study guide timeline places the action around 1987 (Enid returning for Mooma's funeral 1987, Viv going to university 1987, Del having her baby 1988) and puts Enid's last visit to Jamaica in 1982, in the past. The knowledge check therefore marked a defensible answer (1987) wrong. The Easter Monday detail is unverified rather than proven false, but it is a stage-direction-style claim a student might quote, so it has been removed.
findings.evidence: AQA's own set-text page for Leave Taking: 'set in North London', first produced 1987, no year given; Oak National Academy introduction lesson: 'set in London during the 1980s'; Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract, 'Broader passage of time' timeline; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser (no year).

findings.claim: Enid brings both daughters to Mai for a reading - her stated concern is about a letter she received from her sister Cynthia in Jamaica saying that their mother is seriously ill and asking for money ... Enid's other worry - which she shares cautiously - is about Del's behaviour.
findings.truth: The emphasis is reversed. Enid's stated concern in Scene 1 is Del, who has been staying out late and whom Enid already suspects is pregnant. The money is a secondary thread: Enid tells Mai how hard she finds her sister's constant requests, and Mai advises her to send it anyway. There is no letter saying Mooma is seriously ill.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 1: 'Enid is concerned as her eldest daughter, Del, has been staying out late and Enid suspects that she is pregnant'; Nick Hern study guide, Scene Three note: 'Enid's doubts expressed in Scene One about the constant requests for money'.

findings.claim: Mai reads Enid's palm and tells her she will make a long journey. This prediction introduces the possibility of reconciliation... (Flashcard: 'What does Mai predict when she reads Enid's palm in Scene 6?' - 'That Enid will make a long journey.')
findings.truth: There is no palm reading and no long-journey prediction in Scene 6. Enid comes to Mai's, admits her grief over Mooma and her fear for Del, and lets out a howl of pain. Mai gives her something for the stress but refuses to say where Del is, and answers her with a definition of home - that if you are at peace with yourself you are at home anywhere. After Enid leaves, Mai tells Del she should go back to her mother. The only palm readings in the play are Mai reading Del's (Scene 5), Del reading Mai's (Scene 8) and Del reading Enid's (the closing image).
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 6: 'Mai gives Enid something for the stress but doesn't tell her where Del is. After Enid leaves, Mai tells Del she should return to her mother'; Oak National Academy 'An exploration of Scene Six' (Enid's howl of pain, Mai on home; no reading recorded).

findings.claim: Del becomes pregnant during this section of the play [Scenes 4-7] ... Enid's worry about Del in Scene 1 ... is later confirmed.
findings.truth: Del is already in the early stages of pregnancy when the play opens. Enid suspects it in Scene 1 - it is why she takes Del to Mai. The pregnancy becomes open later; it does not begin mid-play. Getting the order wrong weakens any structural argument about Scene 1 as exposition.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, character note: 'Del: Enid's 18-year-old daughter. She is in the early stages of pregnancy'; Scene 1: 'Enid suspects that she is pregnant'.

findings.claim: Brod ... has lost contact with his children (lesson 2); 'has children he no longer sees' (lesson 5); 'his estrangement from his children' (lesson 3 mark scheme).
findings.truth: Brod has a wife and children in Jamaica, whom he visits. He is disenchanted and drinks, but he is not estranged from his family; his ties back home are part of what makes him the play's Caribbean conscience.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy, 'The presentation of the male characters in Leave Taking' (AQA): Brod 'has a wife and children in Jamaica whom he visits'.

findings.claim: She is a first-generation Jamaican immigrant who came to England around 1959 ... (Flashcard: 'Around 1959, as part of the Windrush generation.')
findings.truth: The play does not date Enid's arrival. 1959 is the year Winsome Pinnock's own mother migrated from Jamaica, which Pinnock gives in an interview about the play's origins - it is the playwright's biography, not the character's. Enid is described only as having come to England as a young woman.
findings.evidence: Winsome Pinnock, 'Reaching out for life in a new country' (Nick Hern Books blog, 23 May 2018): her mother 'migrated from Jamaica to the UK in 1959'; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser: 'Enid came to England as a young woman having left her family in Jamaica'.

findings.claim: Mai, who is dying, has given Del her notebook ... 'Mai is not simply dying'; 'clearly dying by the end' (lesson 5); 'it is clear she is dying' (lesson 3); flashcard 'What does Mai give Del before she dies?'; lesson 4 description 'Mai's departure'.
findings.truth: Mai does not die, and there is no departure. She is unwell - a dizzy spell in Scene 5, and in Scene 8 Del reads her palm, senses a health problem and tells her to see a doctor, which Mai deflects. She hands over the notebook because she has no daughter of her own to pass her knowledge to, not because she is dying. The notebook itself is correct.
findings.evidence: WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 8: 'Mai giving Del her notebook as she does not have her own daughter to pass her knowledge on to'; Nick Hern study guide, Scene Eight: 'Del detects that Mai may have some health complications, after reading her palm, and tells her that she should go and see a doctor. Mai avoids the conversation'; Oak, Scene Five: Mai's dizzy spell.

findings.claim: Her mother called her 'Miss English', mocking Enid's assimilation (lesson 2); 'Enid's mother called her Miss English' (lesson 5); flashcard keyed to the mother.
findings.truth: It is her friends and family back in Jamaica, in Scene 3, who call Enid 'Miss English'. Pinning it on Mooma alone narrows a community judgement into a private one and mis-sources a quotation a student may use.
findings.evidence: Oak National Academy, 'Enid's relationships with Jamaica and England' (AQA): 'Enid's friends and family in Jamaica call her Miss English (Scene Three)'.

findings.claim: Enid must face what she has suppressed, Del must choose whether to allow Enid back into her life, and Viv must prepare for her departure to university [in Scene 8].
findings.truth: Viv is not in Scene 8. The scene has only Del, Mai and Enid on stage; Viv's university place is reported by Enid. A student writing about Viv's presence in the final scene would be marked wrong on the text.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide, Scene Eight: 'Who's in it? Del, Mai and Enid'; WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, Scene 8 (Del, Mai, Enid only).

findings.claim: 'no matter how hard I search for myself in them books, I'm never there.' (lesson 5 content and flashcard; paraphrased in lesson 3 as 'no matter how hard I search for myself in these books').
findings.truth: The line is 'But no matter how much I search for myself in them books, I'm never there' - Viv, Scene 5. 'Hard' for 'much' is a one-word misquotation of the unit's single most quotable line.
findings.evidence: Quoted as Viv, Scene 5, in the widely used GCSE quotation sets for Leave Taking; corroborated across two independent searches of the same passage.

findings.claim: All 48 practice questions are labelled '20 marks - Whole Text Essay' or '20 marks - Extract Comparison' and stamped [20 marks], with band descriptors keyed to a 20-mark scale (Top band 17-20 / Mid band 9-16 / Lower band 1-8). Fifteen of them ask students to 'Compare how Pinnock and the unseen writer present ...'.
findings.truth: The modern-text question is a single essay chosen from two, worth 30 marks plus 4 for SPaG. There is no extract, no second text and no unseen comparison anywhere in Section A - the unseen comparison on this paper is a poetry task and has nothing to do with Leave Taking. The fifteen comparison questions are tasks that cannot be set on this text; the mark totals and every band range were wrong. All 48 relabelled to '30 marks - Modern Text Essay', stamped [30 marks], the fifteen comparison prompts rewritten as single-text essays, and band ranges rescaled to Top band (25-30) / Mid band (13-24) / Low band (1-12).
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Paper 2 Questions: 'Section A Modern texts: students will answer one essay question from a choice of two'; 'Section C Unseen poetry'. Paper 2 is 96 marks in total (30+4, 30, 24+8).

findings.claim: When the National Theatre produced the play in 1994, it was the first time a Black British woman's play had been staged there.
findings.truth: Both dates circulate and neither is wrong enough to edit. The National Theatre production opened on 8 December 1994 at the Gulbenkian Theatre, Canterbury, and reached the Cottesloe with a tour running into March 1995. Nick Hern's own study guide says Pinnock was the first Black British woman to have a play produced at the National Theatre 'when Leave Taking was revived there in 1995'. The significance claim itself is correct.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide extract, Introduction; Wikipedia, Leave Taking (production history).

findings.claim: She charges no fee for Enid's final reading, out of sympathy.
findings.truth: Not corroborated by any board, publisher or Oak resource consulted. It may be right, but nothing found supports it, and the sequence they do record is that Mai manoeuvres Del into taking the appointment with Enid. Left unedited; worth a look against the text if anyone has a copy.
findings.evidence: Absent from the WJEC/Eduqas knowledge organiser, the Nick Hern study guide Scene Eight summary and the Oak Scene Eight lesson.

findings.claim: Flashcard: 'Who is Del's first client as an Obeah practitioner?' - 'Enid, her own mother.'
findings.truth: Enid is Del's first named client but not strictly her first. Earlier in Scene 8 Del has already cleaned the room and attended to one of Mai's clients. The dramatic point - that Del's mother is the client Mai steers her towards - survives, so this is not worth an edit.
findings.evidence: Nick Hern Books GCSE study guide, Scene Eight: 'Del has cleaned the room and attended to one of Mai's clients ... Mai dupes Del into having an appointment with Enid'.

findings.claim: Pre-existing validator risk, not a factual error: the descriptions on lessons 3 (105 characters) and 5 (100 characters) are at or over the 100-character limit. Nothing in this pass touches them.
findings.truth: If the edit applier re-validates the whole row on write, these two lessons could be rejected for a reason unrelated to the fact-check. Trim them if the write fails.

summary: Fifteen real findings across all eight lessons, plus four notes. The worst are exam-shaped: lesson 8 tells students they will get a printed extract when the modern-text question is closed book with no extract, and every one of the 48 practice questions carries a 20-mark label, 20-mark band ranges and (in fifteen cases) an unseen-comparison task that this board never sets on a modern text. The worst content errors are the claim that Enid speaks standard English when she speaks Jamaican patois throughout, a fabricated Scene 6 palm reading and long-journey prediction, the death of Mooma reported by letter when it arrives by telephone, Scene 5 placed at Enid's house when it is at Mai's, Mai described as dying when she does not die, and a play set in 1984 when no source dates it beyond the 1980s. 213 surgical edits written; no lesson is clean.
